profiles.meeting_scenario: A partner-level troubleshooting meeting at a Hanoi law firm advising a Vietnamese state-owned project company on a stalled EPC dispute under a FIDIC Yellow Book-based contract for a wastewater treatment plant. The client expected a standing Dispute Avoidance/Adjudication Board-style mechanism to keep claims from escalating, but several variation and extension-of-time claims have bypassed the board stage and are now headed toward formal proceedings. The immediate problem is that the dispute-board pathway is not functioning as the project team thought it would. The agenda is to diagnose why the mechanism failed in practice on this project, identify the legal and contractual root cause, and decide what corrective recommendation to send the client before the next claim notice deadline. The expected outcome is a short action plan covering whether the client should reconstitute the board, issue a fresh referral, and amend its template FIDIC-based conditions for future Vietnam projects.

members.name: Nguyen Minh Chau
members.expertise: FIDIC drafting, dispute boards, arbitration strategy, cross-border infrastructure disputes
members.background: Chau trained in Singapore and London before returning to Hanoi, and now leads the firm's construction disputes practice for foreign-funded infrastructure and energy projects using FIDIC-based forms.
members.private_state: Wants to preserve the client's ability to enforce a board-related procedural step later in arbitration and avoid giving advice that implies the project company waived any contractual rights; is also trying to produce guidance that can be reused in the firm's Vietnam FIDIC template update.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the Board' on this file, they mean the contractually appointed standing FIDIC dispute board contemplated from project commencement, even if in practice it has gone dormant.

A 'referral' means a formal contractual submission that triggers the board's decision timeline under the particular-conditions mechanism, not merely a negotiation package or claim dossier sent for discussion.
If the board mechanism is to be 'restored,' that includes curing appointment and procedural defects sufficiently to support later arbitral jurisdiction and admissibility arguments.
The key failure is likely in how the dispute-board clause was adapted into the Vietnam-facing particular conditions rather than in day-to-day claim handling alone.

members.name: Le Thu Ha
members.role: Senior Associate, Vietnamese Construction & Public Procurement
members.expertise: Vietnamese construction law, SOE contracting practice, contract administration, public project compliance
members.background: Ha has spent eight years advising local employers and project management units on implementing imported standard forms within Vietnamese regulatory and administrative constraints, with particular experience on infrastructure projects financed by mixed public and development-bank sources.
members.private_state: Wants to give the client a practical fix that the project management unit can actually implement quickly without reopening politically sensitive procurement approvals; is concerned that an overly formal answer will ignore how the project team has really been operating.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the Board' on this project, they mean the ad hoc three-person panel the parties discussed constituting after the first major variation dispute, because no standing board ever functioned operationally.

A 'referral' includes the claim package already escalated through the engineer and then shared with proposed board candidates and the other side, since that is how project personnel commonly understand escalation in practice.
If the mechanism is 'fixed,' it is enough that the next live dispute can be channelled through a workable expert panel process that reduces escalation, even if the historical chain is imperfect.
The main root cause is operational incompatibility between FIDIC-style dispute-board administration and Vietnamese approval, budget, and appointment practices on state-linked projects.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether 'the Board' was ever properly in place and how to get 'the Board' working again.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the standing contractual dispute board envisaged under the FIDIC-based contract from the start of the project.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the later ad hoc panel the project team tried to assemble once disputes had already crystallized.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: On FIDIC matters, 'the Board' is a routine shorthand that sounds unambiguous to both lawyers; each assumes the file history obviously points to the same body, so neither pauses to distinguish standing versus post-dispute constitution.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the next step should be to 'make a referral to the Board' before matters escalate further.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a formal notice and submission satisfying the contractual prerequisites and triggering the board's decision timetable under the particular conditions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means packaging the existing claim record and sending it into the board track in a practical sense, even if earlier notice defects or appointment irregularities are not fully cured first.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In construction disputes, 'referral' often functions as a common-sense verb rather than a carefully defined term in conversation, so both hear operational agreement while importing different levels of formality.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both frame the meeting around how to 'fix' or 'restore' the dispute-board mechanism for the client.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 will count it as fixed only if the chosen path preserves a defensible contractual dispute-board step that can withstand scrutiny in later arbitration or enforcement.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 will count it as fixed if the client gets a workable process for the current claims cycle that is administratively feasible and likely to reduce immediate escalation on the project.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria sound like ordinary legal troubleshooting goals, and in a cooperative internal meeting neither needs to state the yardstick explicitly because 'fixing' seems self-evidently positive.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should send the client 'a recommendation on the board mechanism' after the meeting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the recommendation will include both a project-specific salvage plan and template-level drafting changes for future Vietnam FIDIC contracts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the recommendation is limited to immediate steps on this project file, avoiding broader template reform unless separately requested.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Law-firm troubleshooting calls often move fluidly between matter-specific advice and precedent-building lessons, so 'recommendation' naturally carries different implicit boundaries without sounding inconsistent.

turns.inner_thought: The client wants an answer that does two things at once: salvage the dispute-board step on this wastewater plant matter and give us something reusable for the Vietnam FIDIC update. I need to keep the advice from sounding like they already lost or waived the Board route. When I say the Board, I mean the standing contractual body that should have existed from the start, even if nobody treated it properly. And if we are going to restore it, it has to be in a way that can still be defended later if this ends up in arbitration.
turns.utterance: Let me frame it. The client wants to know why the Board mechanism did not stop these wastewater-plant claims drifting toward arbitration, and what recommendation on the board mechanism we should send this week. For me, the questions are where the process broke down, whether the Board was ever really in place, and how we fix it without creating a worse problem later.

turns.inner_thought: From the file, the real story is that nobody had any functioning board process until the first major variation fight, then the project team scrambled to identify three names. Chau is probably thinking in standard-form logic, but the operational history here is much messier. When I refer to the Board, I mean that later panel the parties tried to put together once the claims became serious.
turns.utterance: On the timeline, the first major variation dispute sat with the engineer for quite a while, then the EOT issues followed, and by the time the determinations came out both sides were already entrenched. Only after that did the parties start trying to line up members for the Board, while also circulating the claim materials and technical backup. So by the time the Board entered the picture, the claims had already hardened quite a bit.

turns.inner_thought: That confirms my concern: if the standing Board was never truly operational from project commencement, the appointment provisions in the particular conditions may be the real defect. I need to test whether the clause was drafted in a way that broke the FIDIC logic. If the contractual machinery itself is unsound, merely getting people around a table now will not fix the mechanism in the sense I care about.
turns.utterance: Yes. If the Board was never really operational from the start, then the first issue for me is whether the appointment machinery in the particular conditions was defective. We need to separate a problem in administration from a problem in the clause itself, because that affects how we think about restoring the mechanism.

turns.inner_thought: I do not think the answer is mainly defective drafting. On paper, the clause was serviceable enough. The real problem was that a state-linked project company was never going to secure approvals, budget sign-off, and comfort on retainers before there was a visible dispute. And in practice they have already treated the shared claim bundle as a referral of sorts. What matters now is getting something workable, not rebuilding the theory of the file.
turns.utterance: My sense is the mechanism looked workable on paper, but in practice the project company could not get internal approvals for retainers or recurring costs, so nobody moved until there was an actual dispute to refer. By then, the team was treating the escalation materials as the start of the Board process anyway. So part of the failure was less legal design and more how the project had to operate day to day.

turns.inner_thought: We should still tell them to make a referral to the Board now, but only if the contractual sequence can be defended: notice, engineer stage, time bars, and whatever the particular conditions require. I do not want advice that implies the earlier informal circulation already counted, because that could prejudice later admissibility arguments.
turns.utterance: Understood. I think the immediate step is still to make a referral to the Board now, but only after we check whether the prior notices and the engineer determinations line up with the contractual sequence. If we are going to put the client back onto that track, I want the steps taken in the right order.

turns.inner_thought: That is fine. From my perspective, the practical job is to turn the existing claim record into a referral package and get the panel engaging quickly. I am assuming the earlier engineer-stage materials and what was already circulated can be folded in, rather than reopening every historical defect. The client needs something implementable before the next deadline.
turns.utterance: Agreed in principle. We can compile the existing claim file, the correspondence, the engineer-stage record, and the delay and variation schedules into a referral package so the Board can start engaging quickly. If we organise it properly, the client should be able to move without recreating the whole history from scratch.

turns.inner_thought: I should steer this toward the deeper drafting issue, because I suspect the Vietnam-specific amendments imported board language but stripped out the standing-board architecture. That matters not only for this case but also for our template update. The recommendation on the board mechanism should not be confined to project triage.
turns.utterance: Stepping back, I do think the deeper problem may be the Vietnam-specific amendments. They seem to have imported the language of a dispute board without preserving the full appointment logic behind it. So when we diagnose why this failed, we should look carefully at what was changed in the particular conditions and not only at the project team's handling.

turns.inner_thought: I do not disagree that the drafting can be improved, but I think Chau is overweighting the text. On these projects, the real friction is approval pathways, cost controls, and cultural resistance to appointing a board before anyone sees a live dispute. Fixing the mechanism, for me, means giving the project company a process it can actually run now.
turns.utterance: I agree the amendments deserve a look, but I would not put everything on the wording. The larger friction on projects like this is local approval practice, payment control, and general discomfort with appointing the Board before any visible dispute exists. Even a cleaner clause can stall if those practical constraints are not addressed.

turns.inner_thought: We need both outputs. I want the note to restore the Board path on this file in a legally robust way and also to capture drafting changes for future Vietnam FIDIC contracts. If we only send immediate operational steps, we miss the precedent value and leave the same defect alive.
turns.utterance: That is fair. So the recommendation on the board mechanism should cover both how to restore the Board path on this project and what drafting changes the client should make in future Vietnam FIDIC-based templates. The file is giving us a current problem and a systemic lesson.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with mentioning future lessons, but the client mainly needs a practical note for this project. My action items are to get the Board constituted now, secure a procedural agreement everyone can live with, and move the present claims through that channel. I do not want the note to become an abstract template reform exercise.
turns.utterance: Yes, we can mention future lessons, but I would keep the action items focused on this project: constituting the Board now, getting a procedural agreement in place, and moving the current disputes through that channel. That is the part the project management unit can actually act on immediately.

turns.inner_thought: I will split the memo so I can control the formal analysis on validity of a referral under the present clause, and also include wording revisions for later deals. I need a careful section on whether a proper referral can still be made now under the existing contract architecture.
turns.utterance: Good. Let us divide it that way. I will take a short memo section on whether a formal referral can still be validly made under the current clause, and I also want a section on revisions to the dispute-board wording for later deals. That should give the client both immediate guidance and a cleaner path going forward.

turns.inner_thought: I will draft the chronology and the practical steps to get the board mechanism working again before the deadline. In my mind, that means pulling together the factual record, getting the panel into place, and setting up a workable process for the live claims cycle. I am assuming the recommendation is mainly file-specific, even if Chau adds broader drafting comments.
turns.utterance: Understood. I will draft the factual chronology and the practical steps for getting the board mechanism working again before the client's next claim deadline. I will also set out what needs to happen on appointments, approvals, and the materials to be sent so the process can start moving.
